paras: The lynching of Case Jones was the killing of a Black man by a mob at Elk Valley, Tennessee, on the morning of June 24, 1903. Jones was accused of assaulting a young white girl, Margaret Bruce, the day before, and was hanged after being taken from a deputy sheriff. An Associated Press brief carried the story to papers across the country, and Black weeklies reprinted it and listed Jones among the month's lynchings.

According to a Knoxville dispatch in the New York Sun, Jones was 22 years old and worked on a construction train of the Southern road. The Sun placed Elk Valley in Campbell county, forty miles north of Knoxville. Most papers named him "Case Jones", while the Sun called him "Charles Jones" and the San Antonio Daily Light "Charles L. Jones".

Jones was charged with an assault on Margaret Bruce, daughter of a farmer, Charles Bruce, late on the afternoon of Tuesday, June 23, while she was picking berries with her sister. The Associated Press called it a "criminal assault" on a 12-year-old, while the Sun described an "attempted assault" on a thirteen-year-old. In the wire version, Jones was caught during the night, taken before the girl, who identified him, and "broke down and confessed".

The Sun gave a different sequence after the arrest. Deputy Sheriff Calvin May was waiting with Jones for a train at Pioneer to take him to "Jacksonboro jail" when a mob of "less than fifty citizens of Campbell county" seized him and hanged him to a tree at 5 a.m. The Associated Press said he was "strung up a tree at daylight" and that his body was "riddled with bullets", a detail the Sun did not mention.
The Sun reported that no arrests had been made and that "the indications are that none will be." No report of an inquest, indictment or trial appears in the coverage.

The Associated Press dispatch, datelined Elk Valley, ran on June 24 and 25 from New York to Texas, Iowa, Minnesota, Virginia and the Dakotas, usually as a short telegraph item. Headlines took the accusation and confession as settled: "Negro Brute Lynched" in San Antonio, "Mob Makes Short Work of Child's Assailant" in Minneapolis, "Admitted His Crime and Was Hanged" in Richmond. Weekly digests in early July shortened it further, the River Falls Journal writing that a mob had lynched Jones, "who assaulted a 12-year-old girl". Only the Sun printed a separate Knoxville account, which named the deputy and the county and noted that no one was expected to be arrested.

The Black press carried the same wire text without comment. The Wisconsin Weekly Advocate ran it on June 25 as "Negro Confesses and Is Lynched", grouped with reports of mobs at Peoria, East St. Louis and in Mississippi, and the Cleveland Gazette printed it unheaded among general news two days later. Black papers then entered the case in their running counts: the Indianapolis Freeman's list of June lynchings, the Wichita Searchlight's list with the charge, the Seattle Republican's tally in August, and the Chicago Broad Ax's chronology of the year. White papers kept similar lists, the Pine Bluff Daily Graphic printing its under the heading "Number of Lynchings Increasing Throughout North and South".

The two dispatches differ on the victim's first name, the girl's age, whether the charge was assault or attempted assault, whether Jones confessed, and whether his body was shot. The Sun's account is the more detailed of the two, naming the officer, the place of seizure and the county, but it is the only report of the custody and the size of the mob.

accounts.label: Knoxville dispatch (New York Sun)
accounts.gist: A mob of fewer than fifty Campbell county citizens seized Jones from Deputy Sheriff Calvin May at Pioneer, where May was waiting for a train to the jail, and hanged him to a tree at 5 a.m.; the charge was attempted assault on a thirteen-year-old; no confession or shooting is mentioned and no arrests were expected.

framing.detail: Headlines called Jones a 'Negro brute' and 'child's assailant' and spoke of 'swift punishment', treating the confession as settled.
Most papers ran the AP text as a brief among telegraph news; some digests dropped 'accused' and stated the assault as fact.
The Sun's dispatch used 'charged against' and 'attempted assault' and reported that no arrests were expected.
The Wisconsin Weekly Advocate and Cleveland Gazette reprinted the AP text, the Advocate beside other mob items; neither added comment.
Black papers kept the case in running lynching tallies ('Case Jones, colored, Elk Valley, Tenn.'), the Freeman under a note that June 'sustains its reputation' as a month of fatalities.
